item.title: State Opens Homicide Investigation Into Police Killing of Madison Man
item.description:
State officials in Wisconsin have opened a homicide investigation into a fatal shooting of a Black man by a police officer in Madison on Wednesday that was captured on video and set off protests in the city.

At an acrimonious news conference on Thursday that was disrupted repeatedly and, during one stretch, taken over completely by one protester, the Madison police chief pledged he would cooperate fully with state investigators.

“We will not hide from any aspect of this investigation,” Chief John Patterson said. He added that the police department would review its training and use of force policy.

The killing occurred on Wednesday afternoon on a busy street in the Marquette neighborhood, near the State Capitol, where officers were responding to reports of a person stealing bicycles and trying to enter parked vehicles, officials said. The police approached the man, who pulled out a knife during an ensuing struggle, they said.

Officers tried to incapacitate the man with a Taser, but it was deployed unsuccessfully, Chief Patterson, said. An officer who was injured by the knife fired at the man, who was taken to a hospital and died. Three other officers were involved, and one of them was also injured during the struggle, but it was unclear how, Chief Patterson said. He added that the injury did not appear to be from the knife. All four officers have been placed on administrative leave, he said.

In a video of the shooting circulated widely on social media, a man is surrounded by four officers. As three of them try to hold him, one shoots.

Madison’s mayor, Satya Rhodes-Conway, identified the victim during the Thursday news conference as Corey Ruiz, 38. In a news release, Noah Lieberman, a city alderman, identified Mr. Ruiz as Black and called for more police oversight. Police records listed Mr. Ruiz’s race as African American.

The Madison police did not release the name of the officer who fired, but Chief Patterson said he hoped state investigators would release it soon.

“This is an incredibly difficult moment for the Madison community,” Ms. Rhodes-Conway said, adding that “as a city, as a community, as a society, we have to do better.”

On Wednesday evening, hundreds of protesters marched from the Marquette neighborhood to the Capitol, according to local media reports.

On Thursday, people gathered near the shooting site. Some left flowers. Others wrote messages on the street in chalk demanding justice for Mr. Ruiz.

Michele McCoy, 64, a cashier at the Willy Street Co-Op nearby, came to the site to protest, saying she was “devastated and enraged,” and demanded the officer be charged.

At a vigil for Mr. Ruiz on Thursday night, David Ortiz-Wittingham, a local labor organizer, said he had witnessed the encounter as he was driving on Williamson Street. A police car passed him and then another came from the other direction, he said. Then more police cars arrived and an officer exited one and started running.

Mr. Ortiz-Wittingham said that he saw Mr. Ruiz crash while trying to go from the sidewalk to the street on a bike. The police then “swarmed” Mr. Ruiz and tried to restrain him, he said.

“I saw him with his hands behind his back and a cop approaching with what I thought was a Taser,” Mr. Ortiz-Wittingham said. “I thought, ‘OK, they’re trying to Tase him,’ but then another squad car pulled up and blocked my view. About two seconds later another squad car pulled up and I heard the shots.”

Mr. Ortiz-Wittingham, 25, said he had spoken with Madison’s independent police monitor but not yet with anyone from the state. He said he felt he should speak because most police officers in Madison are not equipped with body-worn cameras.

“In the moment, it felt like witnessing an execution,” he said. He added: “Even if the police account is true, I don’t think he should have died. It should have been de-escalated.”

In the same neighborhood, in 2015, a white police officer shot and killed Anthony Robinson, a 19-year-old Black man, and protests followed. The district attorney did not file charges, deeming that the officer’s actions had been justified. In 2012, Paul Heenan, a white man, was fatally shot by the police after he mistakenly entered the wrong home. The same district attorney found the use of deadly force was justified, and the officer was not charged.

Chief Patterson mentioned both of those killings during the Thursday news conference, saying the community had gone through considerable trauma.

He acknowledged that for many people in the city right now, there was a “thinness of trust” with city officials.

“I can feel it,” he said.

Chief Patterson said the footage seen by many on social media was only “one perspective” of what had transpired and added that “not all perspectives are online right now.” He also sought to dispel an online rumor and emphasized that Mr. Ruiz did not appear to have been placed in handcuffs before he was shot.

The news conference on Thursday turned chaotic when some protesters stormed in and began to interrupt Mr. Patterson, saying the city was corrupt. One man, Carlos Dixon, a write-in candidate for Wisconsin governor, seized the microphone and demanded that the officers involved be put in jail immediately.

“There should be accountability,” he demanded.

City officials, including Chief Patterson, allowed Mr. Dixon to speak for several minutes.

After state investigators complete their investigation, they will share their findings with the district attorney’s office, who will decide whether to bring charges against the officer, Chief Patterson said.

Mr. Ruiz’s family members did not respond to requests for comment on Thursday. Sabrina Madison, a city alderwoman, said she believed Mr. Ruiz was a father. Public records showed a Madison address as his residence. He had a criminal record that included convictions for drug possession, theft and resisting or obstructing an officer, records showed.

At the vigil on Thursday, several hundred gathered, with people chanting Mr. Ruiz’s name, giving speeches and singing songs. Many wrote messages in chalk or left candles and bouquets in the street.

Marcus Lane, a 37-year-old butcher, said he had known Mr. Ruiz since high school. He described his friend as a “good guy” who was always willing to help him out.

“He was always just a phone call away, very down to earth,” he said.

Mr. Lane, a Black Madison native, said he was not shocked to hear that the police had shot a Black man.

“Every day I fear for my life when I walk out the house.”

Yan Zhuang and Jacey Fortin contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Administration Drops Subpoena Demanding List of Jews From Penn
item.description:
The Trump administration has for now abandoned its quest to force the University of Pennsylvania to turn over names of Jewish people on campus, according to a court filing on Thursday.

The administration’s retreat does not resolve the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s long-running inquiry into concerns about antisemitism at Penn. But the government’s move appears to spell the end, at least in Penn’s case, of a politically volatile and legally fraught tactic.

The government did not explain its decision in the court filing, and a spokesman for the E.E.O.C. declined to comment.

The move, however, represents a rare pullback by the Trump administration, which has sought to use investigations and funding cuts as tools of leverage against elite universities.

The investigation into Penn began in December 2023, when Andrea Lucas — an E.E.O.C. commissioner appointed by President Trump during his first administration — filed a civil rights charge against the university, citing a “pattern or practice of harassment against Jewish faculty, staff and other employees,” particularly in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas on Israel.

But the investigation gathered force only once Mr. Trump returned to the White House. The E.E.O.C. quickly began pressing Penn to surrender records about antisemitism complaints and a list of “all clubs, groups, organizations and recreation groups” that were “related to the Jewish religion, faith, ancestry/national origin.”

The government also demanded membership rosters of those groups, as well as a list of people who had worked in Penn’s Jewish Studies Program.

Penn complied with some of the government’s requests and balked at others, and the commission sued in November to enforce a subpoena it had issued. The university and its allies warned that the government’s demands were unconstitutional and endangered people.

“The E.E.O.C. insists that Penn produce this information without the consent — and indeed, over the objections — of the employees impacted while entirely disregarding the frightening and well-documented history of governmental entities that undertook efforts to identify and assemble information regarding persons of Jewish ancestry,” the university said in a court filing in January.

The government insisted that it needed the information to investigate antisemitism on Penn’s campus and that the university’s response had been hyperbolic and extreme.

“We’re not looking for a list of Jews or registry of Jews or a catalog of Jews,” Debra Lawrence, a lawyer for the commission, told a judge during a hearing in March. “How about a spreadsheet that identifies the contact information for potential victims and witnesses? That’s all that we’re looking for here.”

The judge, Gerald J. Pappert of Federal District Court in Philadelphia, ruled that month that the university largely had to comply with the subpoena, though he stayed his decision so Penn could appeal.

Judge Pappert’s decision hinted at discomfort with how the commission had pursued its inquiry, particularly with a demand for information tied to groups “related to the Jewish religion.”

Nevertheless, Judge Pappert said, Penn’s constitutional claims were “easily dispensed with” and the school appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

On Thursday, the dispute ended with more surprise than fanfare when the government and Penn filed six pages with the Third Circuit. In the submission, the E.E.O.C. said it would “not take any further measures to enforce the subpoena.” It also pledged not to “otherwise seek from the University of Pennsylvania any material sought by the subpoena” while the current investigation is pending.

The White House did not immediately comment. Penn welcomed the move.

“With the support of many members of the community who have stood with Penn throughout, the university has been able to protect its employees’ rights and none of the subpoenaed personal contact information was disclosed,” Matthew D. Grossman, a university spokesman, said in a statement. “Penn remains committed to fighting antisemitism and all other forms of discrimination, to ensure everyone it serves can learn, work and thrive.”

Only occasionally have universities resisted the Trump administration’s tactics so forcefully. Harvard University and the California State University System brought lawsuits to challenge funding losses or threats of cuts, but few others have fought the administration’s efforts as openly as Penn did.

Still, Penn has had a complex relationship with the Trump administration. Last summer, after the administration paused about $175 million in research funding, Penn settled a civil rights case with the Education Department, which had accused the university of sex discrimination when it allowed a transgender athlete to compete on its women’s swim team years earlier.

The agreement included no financial penalties for Penn, but it prompted a backlash on campus, where people accused leaders of bowing to the Trump administration. At the time of the agreement, Penn’s president, J. Larry Jameson, said that the government’s inquiry had left the university vulnerable to “significant and lasting implications,” referring to the possible loss of federal funding.

The pause on research funding quickly ended, though that was not formally a part of the settlement. By then, though, the university had spent months privately clashing with the E.E.O.C., which had taken on an outsize role in the administration’s crusade to change higher education.

The commission, for instance, was essential to last summer’s settlement between the government and Columbia University. It has also worked on investigations into other top schools, including Cornell University and the University of California system.

In the Penn case, Ms. Lucas’s initial charge was highly unusual because it did not arise from an employee complaint. Ms. Lucas, a Penn alumna who is now the E.E.O.C.’s chair, has used so-called commissioner’s charges in other high-profile investigations, including the agency’s inquiry into Nike over its diversity policies and its charges against Columbia and Barnard College over anti-Jewish harassment.

item.title: Clint Reilly, Political Consultant Known for Feuding, Dies at 79
item.description:
Clint Reilly, a feared and respected political consultant who ran winning campaigns in California, but whose combustible personality sometimes upstaged the candidates he worked for, died on Saturday in San Francisco. He was 79.

His death was announced by The San Francisco Examiner, which Mr. Reilly bought in 2020, two decades after an only-in-San-Francisco feud with the paper’s management. The cause of death, in a hospital, was chronic lung disease, Frank Holland, a family friend, said.

Mr. Reilly advised some of California’s most successful Democrats of the 1980s and ’90s, including Nancy Pelosi, Dianne Feinstein and Barbara Boxer, whose careers all began in the Bay Area. In 1999, he became a candidate himself, running for mayor of San Francisco and finishing fourth after spending $3.5 million of his own money.

The son of a milkman, Mr. Reilly possessed a granular knowledge of voting blocs and an adman’s instinct for distilling a winning message. He was an early adopter of using computers to identify voters by demographics and interests, so they could be targeted individually. His direct-mail and TV ads delivered a visceral punch, often through attacks on opponents.

“The guy’s a genius,” Richard Riordan, a rare Republican client, told The Los Angeles Times after Mr. Reilly guided him to unexpected victory in the 1993 Los Angeles mayoral race.

As the manager of Ms. Pelosi’s first congressional campaign in 1987, Mr. Reilly coined a prophetic slogan for the future House Speaker: “A voice that will be heard.”

But not all of Mr. Reilly’s clients were pleased with his work. In 1989, after managing two successful mayoral races for Ms. Feinstein, he quit her campaign for governor during the Democratic primary while she was recovering from a hysterectomy. Before telling his client, he faxed reporters the news that he was resigning, saying that she wasn’t working hard enough.

“I am free at last,” Ms. Feinstein responded. She went on to win the primary, lose the general election to Pete Wilson, a Republican, and win a U.S. Senate seat in 1992 — all without Mr. Reilly’s help.

Mr. Reilly goaded candidates to spend lavishly to win, with the not-coincidental side effect that his fees were also lavish. After growing up with little, he favored Italian suits, drove a red Jaguar and lived in a three-story house with a view of the Golden Gate Bridge in the upscale Sea Cliff neighborhood of San Francisco.

When Quentin L. Kopp was a San Francisco supervisor, he hired Mr. Reilly to manage his long-shot 1979 mayoral challenge to Ms. Feinstein, the incumbent. Mr. Reilly made his reputation during that campaign, which forced Ms. Feinstein into a runoff. But during the race, he was arrested and charged with driving drunk.

Mr. Kopp’s supporters urged him to fire Mr. Reilly, he recalled in an interview. He refused, and the two remained friends, though he took to jokingly referring to Mr. Reilly as “Satan,” for his volatile temperament. (Mr. Reilly said that he quit drinking soon after the arrest.)

At a holiday party at Mr. Reilly’s home some years later, Mr. Kopp said, “Clint’s mother implored me to stop referring to him as Satan,” which he did.

Mr. Reilly’s purchase of The Examiner followed a long saga in and out of courtrooms, starting in 1993, when he visited the office of the executive editor, Phil Bronstein, to complain about the paper’s coverage of a client and left in an ambulance with a broken ankle.

He sued Mr. Bronstein, claiming that the editor had shoved him; he also sued the newspaper’s publisher, William Randolph Hearst III, who was present during the incident. Mr. Reilly won an undisclosed settlement, and The Examiner expressed regret for his injury.

In 2000, Mr. Reilly was back in court with The Examiner, this time suing its owner, the Hearst Corporation, on antitrust grounds to stop it from buying the rival San Francisco Chronicle.

Lawyers for The Examiner called the suit an attempt to settle old scores, after the newspaper had backed Mayor Willie L. Brown Jr. the previous year during Mr. Reilly’s failed mayoral campaign. A federal judge ruled in favor of Hearst.

Two decades later, after The Examiner had passed through several different owners, Mr. Reilly acquired the newspaper and a sister publication, SF Weekly, for an undisclosed sum. He reinvented The Examiner as a broadsheet that published three days a week, with an accompanying digital site, focused on local news.

After Mr. Reilly left political consulting in 1995, he became a successful commercial real estate investor, starting with his purchase that year of the Merchants Exchange Building downtown for $18 million. He also owned event spaces and hospitality businesses.

Clinton Thomas Reilly was born on Jan. 13, 1947, in Oakland, Calif., the eldest of 10 children of Joe Reilly, who delivered milk for Berkeley Farms, and Bess (Stone) Reilly, who operated a concessions stand at the Oakland Coliseum. He grew up in San Leandro, a working-class city in the East Bay.

At 14, he declared his intention to become a Roman Catholic priest and entered St. Patrick’s Seminary in Menlo Park, earning a bachelor’s degree in philosophy. But after nine years of study, he abandoned his plans, concluding that social justice could be better pursued through politics.

“I think initially, intuitively, I wanted to get involved in politics because that was a place where you could improve people’s lives and make the biggest impact on the direction of the world,” he told The Los Angeles Times in 1994.

His first client was one of his former seminary professors, the Rev. Eugene J. Boyle, a liberal activist who ran unsuccessfully for State Assembly in 1974.

Mr. Reilly married Janet Koewler, a former aide to Mr. Riordan, in 1995. The two met while he was running the Riordan campaign. She survives him, along with two daughters, Jill and Ava Reilly; six brothers, Kevin, Mark, Brian, Joseph, Matthew and Dan; and a sister, Linette Hamil.

Candidates “are not hiring me because they want me to get along with everybody,” Mr. Reilly once told The Los Angeles Times. “The campaign is a war, you know?”

item.title: Tugboat Captain Pleads Guilty in Miami Crash That Killed 3 Children
item.description:
The captain of a 25-foot tugboat that was pushing a barge when it slammed into a sailboat last year in Miami Beach, killing three children from a sailing camp, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to a count of seaman’s manslaughter.

The captain, Yusiel Lopez Insua, 47, of Miami, admitted in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida that his actions caused the collision, according to court documents. He faces up to 10 years in prison.

Prosecutors said Mr. Insua was pushing a barge across Biscayne Bay just before 11:30 a.m. on July 28, 2025, when it struck a stalled sailboat carrying five girls, ages 7 to 13, and a 19-year-old camp counselor. The Miami Yacht Club said the children and the counselor were from a sailing camp run by the Miami Youth Sailing Foundation.

The U.S. Coast Guard received a report that a barge had struck the sailboat near Hibiscus and Monument islands in Miami Beach.

Three of the girls were killed. The Miami-Dade County Medical Examiner’s Office identified two of them as Mila Yankelevich, 7, and Erin Ko, 13. Days later, the family of a third victim, Arielle Buchman, 10, announced that she, too, had died.

Federal prosecutors said that the camp counselor had tried to alert Mr. Insua to the sailboat’s presence, but that his forward view was blocked by part of the tugboat’s structure.

“Three children lost their lives in a tragedy that never should have happened,” Jason A. Reding Quiñones, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, said in a statement.

Mr. Insua’s lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: ‘Heartbreaking’ Video Shows Bear Before It Was Electrocuted Atop Utility Pole
item.description:
Shannon Mullens was driving with her family on a desolate highway in rural New Mexico on Monday morning when they spotted a black bear on top of a utility pole. It was about 22 feet off the ground, panting heavily near wires that carry 7,200 volts.

Ms. Mullens recorded a video of the bear as her fiancé called 911. The dispatcher told them to leave the bear alone and added that there was nothing the authorities could do because it could fall if they tried to tranquilize it or coax it down.

“It was shocking but also heartbreaking,” Ms. Mullens said in an interview on Thursday. “We just felt helpless. There was nothing we could do to help the guy out.”

By the time a utility crew and a sheriff’s deputy arrived at the pole east of Gladstone, an unincorporated community in northeast New Mexico, the bear had been electrocuted, Sheriff Curtis Skaggs of Union County, N.M., said in an interview. Its body was on the ground.

“The best thing we could have done is move people back and give it some breathing room and maybe we wouldn’t have had this unfortunate situation,” he said.

Video footage of the stranded bear, which circulated widely this week, highlighted the danger wild animals face when they come into contact with high-voltage power lines and other utility infrastructure. Scientists said that problem could become more persistent with accelerated land development and climate change.

Jon Holst, a wildlife expert with Western Resource Advocates, a nonprofit that fights climate change, said bears had been moving into more areas of the West this year, in part because the extremely dry winter deprived them of the foods they eat in their usual habitats.

“As climate change causes these sorts of extreme events to happen more, it’s going to become more common, which is unfortunate,” he said. “Bears are going into areas where they don’t normally go.”

David Spradlin, the chief executive of Springer Electric Cooperative, which owns the utility pole that the bear ascended, said the animal might have been spooked by a car on Highway 56, which is nearby.

“I wouldn’t say it’s common, but it does happen,” Mr. Spradlin said. He added that with drought conditions, “we are seeing them more and more in areas where we’ve never really had issues with them.”

In addition to seeking shelter from threats, bears are attracted to the creosote and tar that some utility poles are soaked in, said Tom Smith, a professor of wildlife sciences at Brigham Young University who has studied the animals for 32 years. Black bears are also exploratory by nature and are expert climbers, he said.

Bears that climb poles usually come down on their own, Mr. Spradlin said. He recalled one time when one of his crews left bacon at the base of a pole to coax one particularly recalcitrant bear to the ground.

Late last year, a lineman in Arizona went up in a cherry picker and used a rod to gently prod a bear down from a utility pole.

In the episode near Gladstone this week, the bear might have been scared to climb down because people had gathered around it to take photos and videos, according to the New Mexico Department of Wildlife, which responded to calls about the bear.

Although people had been instructed to leave the animal alone, “some members of the public continued to stop next to the power pole to film and take pictures of the bear, so the bear remained at the top of the pole,” the department said in a statement.

If animals touch two wires simultaneously, they can be electrocuted, so small birds are usually unharmed, said James Dwyer, a wildlife biologist at EDM International, a consulting firm that works with electric companies. Larger animals like hawks and bears are at greater risk, he said.

Ms. Mullens, who was traveling home to Oklahoma when she saw the bear, said her family drove away before it fell. But she was still haunted by the encounter.

“Even after I got home, I could not get that bear out of my head,” she said. “And hearing that the bear didn’t make it was heartbreaking.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Trump-Thune Rift Intensifies Over Stalled Election Bill
item.description:
The long-simmering tension between President Trump and Senate Republicans over a stalled voting restriction bill intensified on Thursday, after the president’s spokeswoman said that Mr. Trump’s “patience is running out” with Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, for failing to push it through.

Mr. Thune, who has faced criticism from Mr. Trump and his far-right allies for months, quickly fired back, telling reporters that if the White House wanted to see action on the federal elections overhaul — which has neither the majority it would need to pass nor the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster — somebody in the president’s orbit should make a more concerted effort to garner the necessary support to advance it.

“Maybe she or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes,” Mr. Thune said at the Capitol, referring to Karoline Leavitt, the spokeswoman who had told reporters of Mr. Trump’s dwindling patience.

“It’s 50 around here,” Mr. Thune added, referring to the minimum number of votes Republicans need to pass legislation. “And, so, instead of pointing the finger at Republicans, they might think about going after the people who are stopping it on the floor, which is the Democrats. And if there are Republicans that they think are gettable, get on the phone. Let’s get them to ‘yes.’ ”

The back-and-forth was the latest flare-up of an extraordinary intraparty fight over the elections measure, the SAVE America Act, which Mr. Trump has called his top priority.

With the midterm elections approaching in November, Republicans have been eager to present a unified front. Instead, the president’s intense focus on the bill has divided his party, prompting repeated squabbling that has threatened the G.O.P.’s ability to pass legislation despite its majorities in both chambers of Congress.

“I don’t know who it was that sold the president on this idea that this was attainable,” said Senator John Cornyn, a Texas Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger. “But it’s creating a circular firing squad for Republicans, and here we are — what, 103 days before the midterm elections? — and this is not a great place for us.”

The escalating battle will likely complicate the Senate’s final two weeks before their August recess. Mr. Thune already faced a difficult to-do list, laid at his feet by House Republicans who departed Washington for their five-week break on Thursday after having pushed through several bills that face dim prospects in the Senate.

Before senators depart Washington, Republicans are hoping to confirm Mr. Trump’s picks for director of national intelligence and attorney general. The House also sent over a stopgap spending bill to avoid a government shutdown at the end of September. And many Republican senators are also hoping to find a way to provide additional military funding for the war in Iran. But with Democrats opposed to both of those measures, Senate Republicans are unlikely to be able to move either.

Mr. Trump’s proposed elections overhaul would require Americans to show proof of citizenship to register to vote, impose a nationwide voter identification requirement and severely limit voting by mail.

With Democrats uniformly opposed, Mr. Trump has for months tried to cow Republican senators into eliminating or weakening the filibuster so they can ram the bill through with a simple majority vote.

“It’s like, the Senate is a place you send things when you want them to die,” Mr. Trump said at an event in Georgia on Wednesday. “We can’t do this — we’re not going to take this any longer, we’re not going to take it. I’m trying to be nice.”

Then, he directed his attention to Mr. Thune.

“Everybody call John Thune at the Senate,” Mr. Trump told a crowd of supporters. “He’s the leader of the Republican Party, and tell him to get this stuff approved.”

But a Republican majority does not exist in the Senate to do what the president wants. Many G.O.P. senators oppose changing the filibuster rules, and a few object to provisions of the voting bill itself, including the changes to mail-in voting used widely throughout the country, particularly in right-leaning rural areas.

“We just don’t have the votes, and so there’s nothing that Senator Thune can do to change that,” Mr. Cornyn told reporters on Thursday.

Nevertheless, a far-right faction of House Republicans has added to the pressure, threatening to block legislation and then successfully demanding that Speaker Mike Johnson append a version of the SAVE America Act to every major bill it sends to the Senate. This week, they adopted a $95 billion budget plan to fund the war with Iran that would also incentivize states to impose Mr. Trump’s election restrictions.

Mr. Thune has been skeptical that Senate Republicans have enough votes to pass the budget plan, and he has repeatedly maintained that there is not enough support among Senate Republicans to push through the SAVE Act.

Some of that is Mr. Trump’s own doing. Among the Republicans who oppose either the elections overhaul or eliminating the filibuster are several senators whom he has frequently targeted with his social media broadsides, including Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska; Susan Collins of Maine, who is in a tough re-election fight; and Thom Tillis of North Carolina.

Mr. Tillis, who opted not to run for re-election this year, has repeatedly called efforts to pass the SAVE America Act a waste of time. On Thursday, he reiterated his support for Mr. Thune. “Anybody in the White House who thinks he’s not a good leader isn’t qualified for their job,” he told reporters.

Two other senators, Mr. Cornyn and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, lost their re-election bids after Mr. Trump endorsed challengers, leaving them with little incentive to wholeheartedly back his priorities at the expense of the Senate’s institutional power.

After Mr. Trump went after the Senate and Mr. Thune at his rally this week, his team amplified the remarks, and Ms. Leavitt was asked at a briefing on Thursday whether the president had lost patience with the majority leader.

“His patience is running out,” Ms. Leavitt said of Mr. Trump. “He wants to see as much of the SAVE America passed as possible by the August recess.”

Mr. Thune was left to play down the rift. Later Thursday, he suggested he had not been offended.

“I don’t read a lot into it,” he said. “I think it was a question she got, and she was responding to it. It’s the nature of the beast around here.”

Catie Edmondson contributed reporting.

item.title: A Lakers Jacket, Bought for $3 at Goodwill, Fetches Nearly $90,000 at Auction
item.description:
It was around 7:30 a.m., and Quinn Brown was already at the Goodwill Outlet store outside Portland, Ore. It was a popular spot — there was a line outside every day — and the 19-year-old Mr. Brown wanted to get there before it opened.

Buying cheap thrift-store clothes and reselling them online is Mr. Brown’s full-time job. On this particular January day, Mr. Brown didn’t notice much of interest at first. But then he saw a man holding an old Los Angeles Lakers jacket with the name “Chamberlain” on the back — as in Wilt Chamberlain, the Hall of Fame basketball player.

The man dropped the yellow warm-up jacket back into the bins, and Mr. Brown grabbed it, then bought it for $3.07.

This month, that same jacket sold at a Sotheby’s auction for $89,600.

Chamberlain, who died in 1999, wore the jacket for Game 1 or 2 of the 1972 N.B.A. finals against the Knicks, as well as during the following 1972-73 season — his last before retiring — according to SIA Photo Match, which authenticated the jacket for Sotheby’s. The Lakers beat the Knicks four games to one in the finals, and Chamberlain was the series M.V.P.

For Mr. Brown it was the thrift-store find of a lifetime (his next-most-valuable discovery — a T-shirt featuring the Sub Pop record label that he bought for about $1 — sold for just $250, he said).

In a phone interview this week, Mr. Brown said he initially thought the jacket was a reproduction and might be worth a few hundred dollars. But once he got it home, he realized it might be an original and worth much, much more.

The giveaway, as he told CBS, was its size: The 33-inch-long jacket was far too big for Mr. Brown — almost down to his knees — but perfect for Chamberlain, who was 7-foot-1.

Mr. Brown connected with the Instagram account Bidstitch, which promotes valuable vintage clothing, to give the jacket some visibility. After the jacket was featured on the account, Sotheby’s reached out to Mr. Brown.

The online auction, which ran from July 1 to July 20, attracted 48 bids from 21 bidders, according to Amanda Bass, a Sotheby’s spokeswoman.

The auction house had estimated the jacket would sell for $150,000 to $250,000, and Mr. Brown said he was a little disappointed that it had sold for less. But he was quick to acknowledge his good fortune: “$90,000 is pretty good for a $3 investment,” he said.

(Game-worn jerseys, as opposed to warm-up jackets like the one Mr. Brown found, can sell for much more. The jersey that Chamberlain, considered one of the greatest N.B.A. players ever, wore in Game 2 and 5 of the 1972 finals, for example, sold for $4.9 million in 2023.)

So what will Mr. Brown do with that $90,000? Besides spending some of it on a vacation to Vietnam — which he had planned even before his windfall — it will go into his savings, he said.

Which he can apparently afford to do. Mr. Brown said he had sold over 10,000 items (he declined to disclose his profits) and his expenses are low — he lives with his parents in southwest Portland and does not plan to go to college.

“I’m not in a place where, like, I really need the money,” he said.

Mr. Brown may be one of Portland’s more successful thrifters, but he is certainly not the only one. Mr. Brown, who got into reselling during his junior year of high school (he graduated last year), has 10 close friends who are thrifters, he said, three of whom are going with him to Vietnam. He goes to Goodwill stores about three times a week, he said.

Reselling goods from thrift stores has exploded in the last decade, according to Hayley Platt, a local Goodwill spokeswoman. She said that, on any given day, “a large percentage” of shoppers at the Goodwill store where Mr. Brown found the jacket were young people looking for items to resell.

Ms. Platt said she had no idea how the jacket ended up at the store, one of a handful of outlets in the area known as “Goodwill Bins” for their ubiquitous rows of blue bins piled high with stuff, much of which is sold by the pound. The jacket, which had a dry-cleaning tag affixed to it, was a “mystery,” she said. Hundreds of cars swing by the store every day with donations, she said.

The auction was won by David Kohler, the 64-year-old president of SCP Auctions, which handles auctions of rare sports memorabilia, according to David Randolph, the founder and owner of SIA Photo Match.

Mr. Kohler maintains a vast “Lakers shrine” in his home in Orange County, Calif., as a lifelong fan of the team, he said in a phone interview on Thursday. In all his years of collecting and overseeing auctions, he said, he had never heard of someone stumbling on an item of such value in a thrift store. “That’s what makes this such an incredible story,” he said.

Mr. Brown said he led a “pretty normal life” outside thrifting. He watches sports; he plays recreational games like Spikeball.

But, he said, he couldn’t imagine working a regular job with a set salary, one where giving his all wouldn’t sometimes result in a big payday.

And anyway, thrifting isn’t that hard, he said, and he seems to keep getting better at it: “I just see constant improvement.”

item.title: Number of U.S. Troop Deaths Suddenly Appears Lower on Pentagon Website
item.description:
On Wednesday, the Pentagon reported on its casualties website that a total of 18 American service members had been killed during the war in Iran.

By Thursday, the Defense Department had lowered that number, reporting that 14 American troops had been killed in the war.

Three military officials said that one reason behind the change was that the Trump administration decided to remove four service members killed this past weekend from the list — three in Jordan and one in northern Iraq — because their deaths occurred after President Trump declared a cease-fire in the war in April.

The officials described sensitive internal discussions on the condition of anonymity.

The acting press secretary for the Pentagon, Joel Valdez, attributed the change instead to “temporary data disruptions” on the website that he suggested would be quickly fixed.

Since the cease-fire collapsed, the Pentagon has provided little information about the American military strategy and has been slow to release information about troops’ injuries. The last major Pentagon briefing on the war was in early May.

The Defense Department has said that disclosing Iranian strikes on bases where U.S. troops are housed would compromise operational security.

The Pentagon withheld information about three Iranian strikes last week in Jordan that injured dozens of U.S. service members and damaged several helicopters, according to several U.S. officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.

After an Iranian strike in Jordan on Friday killed three soldiers, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, Sean Parnell, acknowledged that the number of U.S. military casualties since July 7 had risen to nearly 100.

Defense Department officials say they are bound by law to report troop deaths, but not injuries. Critics, including Democratic senators, say the Trump administration is obligated to inform the public about the conduct of the war.

“The administration seems to have a real hard time being honest about what is going on — not just about casualties, but about the whole war in general,” said retired Lt. Gen. Ben Hodges, a veteran of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, who commanded U.S. forces in Europe at the start of Mr. Trump’s first term.

General Hodges said that downplaying deaths during war indicated “an unwillingness or inability to aggressively learn from mistakes.”

The issue of troop deaths is significant because both President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have essentially made it so. Both men have repeatedly said that their predecessors, President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III, as well as Vice President Kamala Harris, were personally responsible for the deaths of 13 American service members in a suicide attack in Kabul in 2021.

“These people shouldn’t have died,” Mr. Trump told podcaster Lex Fridman in 2024. “They died because of Biden and because of Kamala. They died just like if they pulled the trigger.”

Dozens of Afghans were also killed in the attack at Abbey Gate, a main entryway at Hamid Karzai International Airport, during the chaotic U.S. evacuation from the country.

The Pentagon has indicated it is preparing to release a review of the Afghanistan withdrawal that Mr. Hegseth ordered. That review, led by Mr. Parnell, will “ensure ACCOUNTABILITY to the American people and the warfighters of our great Nation,” Mr. Hegseth wrote last year in announcing the effort.

In its casualty toll for the Iran war, the Pentagon has separated the number of troops killed under fire from those killed in accidents. As of Wednesday, its data showed that 11 service members were killed in hostilities and seven in accidents related to the war.

The seven killed in accidents include the crew of a U.S. military KC-135 refueling aircraft that crashed in Iraq in March, as part of the war campaign in neighboring Iran.

Mr. Valdez said that comparing the troops deaths under the Trump and the Biden administrations was an “attempt to politicize the sacrifices of America’s finest warriors in Iran.”

By Thursday morning, the number of deaths on the site had been changed to 14, with seven classified as hostile.

Mr. Valdez referred to the changes as “site anomalies” and said they were being resolved.

“The department attempted to explain the anomalies to The New York Times ahead of publication, but given their lack of knowledge in this area, they proceeded to write a non-story,” he said in an email, adding: “We remain committed to ensuring the utmost accuracy of all casualty reporting.”

Mr. Trump has continued to refer to the higher number of U.S. troop deaths. In comments on Thursday, he compared the toll from other American wars to the war against Iran, saying that even one death “is too many, but it’s 18.”

On Wednesday, Mr. Trump witnessed the return of the bodies of the four service members at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, calling them “great heroes.”

“All of them said, very strongly, that we can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon, so we’re going to honor them,” Mr. Trump told journalists as he was departing for the dignified transfer.

Later, Mr. Trump took one soldier’s grieving family to his political rally in Georgia.

Peter Feaver, a political science professor at Duke University who studies the military, said the loss of any service member was a tragedy.

“It’s important to remember that every one of those numbers is a personal story,” he added.

Lazaro Gamio contributed reporting.

item.title: Democratic Voters Keep Defying the Party Establishment
item.description:
Democratic voters are sharply divided over the party’s best path forward, but many seem to share at least one sentiment: boiling frustration with the party’s leadership.

The latest example came this week, when Dr. Amish Shah, a moderate Democrat, won a House primary on Wednesday in a battleground district in Arizona. He prevailed over a different moderate Democrat who was heavily backed by the House Democratic campaign arm.

“As you can clearly see, I wasn’t exactly my party’s pick,” Dr. Shah wryly told reporters on Tuesday night. “I was willing to stand up to that establishment, and that’s what the voters of this district want.”

His victory was the third primary defeat since June for the party’s House campaign arm, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which has intensified its interventions in high-profile contested House primaries. And it freshly illustrated the limits — and drawbacks — of Washington’s attempts to wield influence at a moment of fierce anti-establishment sentiment.

In battleground districts in Maine and California, the campaign committee backed centrist candidates whose allies saw them as stronger contenders in the general election. In Arizona, the ideological differences between the candidates seemed less clear.

But the outcomes for the committee’s preferred candidates were ultimately the same.

“Part of the anger that the grass roots has against the Democratic Party is, they think it’s too much of a clique, too much controlled by donors, consultants and insiders,” said Representative Ro Khanna, a California Democrat who has endorsed several left-leaning candidates in contested primaries. “If we want to reconnect and build trust with the grass roots, we need to be clear that the party is neutral.”

The job of the House Democratic campaign arm this year, its backers say, is not to be neutral. It is to regain control of the House of Representatives.

Tim Persico, a former executive director of the D.C.C.C., said that this was hardly the first time the campaign committee had intervened in high-stakes primaries, or ruffled feathers in doing so.

“It’s one of the hardest things you have to do, but they have to make these calls,” he said.

Courtney Rice, a spokeswoman for the committee, said that decisions to add candidates in competitive primaries to its battlefield program, known as Red to Blue, were made in consultation with Democratic officials and local leaders who knew the district best.

“Given Democrats’ big tent, there is not always consensus, but the decisions are never made in a vacuum,” she said. “Strong nominees allow us to spread our resources to more races, expand the battlefield, and deliver Democrats the biggest majority possible.”

Ms. Rice noted that, of the 10 contested Democratic primaries the committee had weighed in on this year, seven of its preferred candidates had won. She pointed to the party’s support for Bob Brooks, the Democratic nominee in a highly competitive Pennsylvania House district, who attracted support from a broad cross-section of Democratic leaders. And she noted its successful intervention for Johnny Garcia, a sheriff’s deputy running in Texas against a progressive activist who called to imprison “Zionists.”

A statement from the Randy Villegas campaign — which prevailed in California over the D.C.C.C.’s preferred candidate — also highlighted collaboration with the committee since the primary.

In Maine’s Second Congressional District, State Senator Joe Baldacci — who did have the support of the D.C.C.C. — was ahead in the initial count of first-place votes but ultimately lost under the state’s ranked-choice voting system.

In an interview, he said the D.C.C.C. backing had been helpful and noted that he was not the only candidate receiving endorsements from national figures. For instance, Mr. Khanna and some national progressive groups had supported Matt Dunlap, the Maine state auditor, who ultimately won the primary.

“I know there was criticism after that because I was getting help from the national party,” Mr. Baldacci said. “It was kind of odd to tar me with that when they were all doing the same thing.”

There are more tests for the party establishment to come.

Some Democrats are furious with the Senate Democratic campaign arm’s interventions in primaries. Its favored candidate in Maine, Gov. Janet Mills, 78, was rejected by voters in favor of the political newcomer Graham Platner, 41. He dropped out this month after a rape allegation, which he denies.

The next major test of establishment power comes in Michigan on Aug. 4. There, the well-funded Representative Haley Stevens has the backing of Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, in the Senate primary over Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive.

While the backlash against the party leadership has seemed especially pronounced on the left, Representative Mark Pocan, a Wisconsin Democrat and a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, sounded sanguine about his House colleagues in an interview on Thursday.

Of the D.C.C.C.’s primary interventions, he said, “Many of us would prefer they not because we think it’s better to let people in individual states make these decisions.”

But he said he thought the committee was largely, and appropriately, focused on general elections.

“I’m going to focus on the 99.9 percent of what’s going to get us a majority,” he said.

item.title: Kagan Says Supreme Court Has Stood Up to Trump in Key Cases
item.description:
One of the Supreme Court’s three liberal justices defended her conservative colleagues on Thursday, insisting the court has not been too deferential to President Trump.

“I think that is a bad rap,” Justice Elena Kagan said during an appearance in Washington State, at an annual gathering of judges and lawyers who work in the judiciary’s Ninth Circuit.

“Is this court very conservative?” she continued. “Does it do a bunch of things that are out of the playbook of the conservative legal movement that I think are deeply wrong? Yes.”

“But,” she added, “is this court kind of a puppet for the current administration? I think definitely not.”

Justice Kagan made the comments as she answered questions posed by an appeals court judge and a lawyer in front of dozens of attendees who work in the nine-state Western region served by the circuit.

Polls have shown declining trust in the institution, and a number of the justices have used recent public appearances to try to defuse the notion that they have become political actors.

Since Mr. Trump returned to office, the court has signed off on a series of his policies on a temporary basis, through emergency orders that have allowed the administration to carry out many of its executive orders even while their legality was being weighed in court.

But Justice Kagan, when asked how she viewed criticism of the court for greenlighting the administration policies, insisted the reality of the court’s record is more nuanced.

In its most recent term, which ended in late June, the Supreme Court cleared the way for a number of long-term conservative goals, she noted. She cited decisions to allow the president sweeping power to fire leaders of independent agencies and to significantly weaken the Voting Rights Act of 1965, a key civil rights law.

But several times, Justice Kagan continued, a majority of the justices joined together to reject Mr. Trump’s initiatives. The justices agreed to invalidate his sweeping emergency tariffs, to strike down his executive order ending birthright citizenship for the children of undocumented immigrants and some temporary foreign visitors and to nix his attempt to fire a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors.

“I don’t see this as a court that is just going to rubber-stamp what the current administration does — quite the opposite,” she said.

Justice Kagan was in the majority in each of those cases, joined by the court’s other two liberal justices but also several justices appointed by Republican presidents. The court’s decisions rejecting those policies infuriated the president.

Mr. Trump lashed out at the justices who rejected his tariffs program, including two justices nominated by him, calling them “fools and lap dogs.”

When Justice Kagan addressed the same conference last year, she used the appearance to express concern about how the court handled a barrage of emergency applications on Trump administration policies.

At the start of Mr. Trump’s second term, he issued a series of executive orders, many of which faced immediate court challenges that quickly arrived at the court on the emergency docket. Applications on that docket, often referred to by critics as the shadow docket, typically come to the justices without full briefing or a robust lower court record, and the justices sometimes rule on applications without explaining their reasoning.

The court, she said then, should “be cautious about acting on the emergency docket.”

At Thursday’s event, Justice Kagan said that she thought the court had “made some improvements” in the past year in how it has handled emergency requests. For instance, she said she believed that the court’s “transparency has become better by a fair bit” because the court has issued more orders that included some reasoning.

Still, she said she believed the court has still been “granting too many of these applications,” creating a “kind of momentum” that has led to the filing of more emergency requests.

The justice’s comments were her first public statements since she testified to Congress earlier this month to ask for millions more dollars in funding for security for the justices. She was joined on Capitol Hill by Justice Amy Coney Barrett, a conservative justice nominated by Mr. Trump, to describe the rising number of threats made against the justices.

On Thursday, she told attendees of the judicial conference that life for a Supreme Court justice has changed since she was appointed to the court in 2010 by President Barack Obama and the justices faced fewer threats.

“I drove myself to work, went out grocery shopping, went to the movies,” she said of her early years on the court. “I did the normal things that people do without any security in sight. I felt like, you know, just like a normal everyday person. And that’s not true for us anymore.”

item.title: Los Angeles Homeless Population Grows Again, After 2 Years of Decline
item.description:
Homelessness increased in Los Angeles over the past year, according to numbers that will be released by the region’s homelessness authority on Friday, setting up Mayor Karen Bass for a fresh round of criticism amid an already bruising re-election campaign.

The city’s homeless population increased by 3.4 percent from last year, based on the most recent point-in-time count, an annual January census of the region’s homeless population, according to two people who were not authorized to release the data before tomorrow’s announcement.

All told, 45,194 people in Los Angeles were counted as homeless this year, a number that includes people in shelters. The number of people sleeping outside in tents, encampments or in vehicles increased by 7.9 percent from last year.

It was an inopportune result for Ms. Bass, who is running for re-election against another Los Angeles Democrat, Councilwoman Nithya Raman. The mayor had previously hailed two years of declines in homelessness, a major accomplishment on a signature issue, but the latest release represented the first full year under her watch in which the homeless count rose.

Across much of Los Angeles County, the numbers increased between 2025 and 2026, although more modestly: The total homeless population in the region served by the count, which includes the city of Los Angeles along with more than 80 other smaller cities, went up by 1.2 percent.

In a statement on Thursday, Ms. Bass blamed a variety of factors outside her purview for the reversal, citing the federal government’s slashing of safety net programs that help people who are teetering on the edge of homelessness. She also said that cuts by the state and ongoing tensions between the city and the county government, which is in charge of mental health care funding, have also been setbacks.

“Despite these headwinds, we have reduced homelessness in Los Angeles by double digits since 2023,” she said, citing the movement of tens of thousands of people into interim housing. She said another 6,000 had been moved indoors through her signature Inside Safe program, which aims to remove some of the city’s most persistent encampments.

The increase was first reported by Fox 11.

Dr. Margot Kushel, director of the Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative at the University of California, San Francisco, said that regardless of Ms. Bass’s performance, she would have been surprised if this year’s numbers did not reflect the significant obstacles local leaders faced over the past year.

“There’s no question that the 2026 count reflects what happened in 2025,” she said. “And there’s no question that 2025 was a really hard year, in particular for Los Angeles.”

Although only one of the two wildfires that devastated the Los Angeles region last year happened in the city limits, Dr. Kushel noted that the displacement of people from thousands of homes had sent them looking for housing in an already overstretched market.

And she said that homeless service providers across the country had been racing to replace or do without federal funding that had been suddenly pulled.

She is concerned about the effects of federal rule changes related to who qualifies for Medicaid and who can get food stamp dollars in the next couple of years, she said.

“I see some things that really worry me out of California’s control and certainly out of any local government’s control,” Dr. Kushel said. “It’s going to create a story of a failed California, even when it’s predictable and it’s not our doing.”

In the longer term, she hopes that statewide efforts to make it easier to build housing will begin to pay off.

Still, homelessness remains a top issue in the Los Angeles mayor’s race. Ms. Bass, who was first elected on promises to aggressively and humanely move people off the streets, has emphasized past results as evidence that her administration’s approach has been working after roughly a decade in which it seemed the problem was intractable.

Even after the two years of decreases, more than 72,000 people remained homeless in the county, a sprawling metropolis home to some 10 million people. Ms. Raman, who has promoted her office’s work on homelessness as a model for the rest of the city, said in a statement that the mayor’s strategy had not focused enough on moving homeless people into permanent housing.

“These results make clear that the mayor’s approach is not working well enough,” she said.

The mayor was forced into a runoff after failing to earn more than 50 percent of votes in the June primary, which indicated lingering frustration among Angelenos about conditions in the city.

After her reputation suffered a catastrophic blow during the 2025 wildfires, she was able to rebuild some amount of good will among voters by fighting against federal immigration raids.

But in recent weeks, residents have been upset by her response to the June 17 warehouse fire in the Boyle Heights neighborhood that sent toxic smoke billowing over the city. Neighbors have been sickened by the stench of rotting food and swarms of vermin that remain.

item.title: Angst, Love and a Longing to Return Home From War
item.description:
On the final calls that Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton made home to North Carolina, the strain of a yearlong deployment that had brought him to the Middle East — and into the thick of the ongoing war in Iran — was beginning to show. He hadn’t been sleeping. His appetite was diminishing. He longed to return home.

Fear had crept into his voice, his wife, Jamiah Swinton, said. “I could always tell, when the tone would change, that something was going on.”

There were drone attacks at Erbil Air Base, in northern Iraq, where he was stationed, he told her, and they kept coming. “There was no peace,” she said.

His last video call to his wife was extra loving, she said, and very short. He asked to see their 4-year-old daughter, but she was at preschool. It had been a year since he last saw them in person.

Four days later, uniformed men arrived at Ms. Swinton’s door to report that her husband had been killed.

Sergeant Swinton was one of 18 U.S. soldiers who have lost their lives since the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. There was a recent high school graduate who was 19 and loved to dance. A 42-year-old father who dreamed of opening his own martial arts studio. A 39-year-old mother of two on her last deployment. And more than a dozen others.

Sergeant Swinton was among four service members whose deaths occurred last week during escalating clashes between U.S. and Iranian forces in the Persian Gulf, where tensions have worsened since the collapse of a cease-fire last month.

The Defense Department said that he died on Saturday during the disposal of an Iranian drone. The episode, a controlled detonation at the Erbil base, is under investigation, the Pentagon said.

Sergeant Swinton, 30, was not involved in the actual detonation but was killed by flying debris from the blast, said a U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.

Sergeant Swinton was assigned to the 108th Air Defense Artillery Brigade at Fort Bragg, in North Carolina.

Ms. Swinton, 27, had been in the Army, too, and she met her husband when both were deployed to Bahrain in 2020. They had different jobs — he watched radar, and she worked on missile launchers — but they gravitated to one another when they had free time.

“What caught my eye was, obviously, how handsome he is,” Ms. Swinton said, adding that he was endlessly goofy and still managed to command respect. “He knew his job so well, and it made people listen to him.”

Ms. Swinton grew up in Southern California. She joined the military because she wanted to see more of the world, and because her mother had also served. Sergeant Swinton, who lived in Fayetteville, told his wife that he had joined the Army because he did not want to get stuck in North Carolina, and that he had been motivated to do well by the birth of his son, now 6.

After meeting in Bahrain, they fell in love fast. They moved to Texas — they had both been stationed there, at Fort Hood — and got married in a courthouse in 2021. They had a daughter, Aleia, now 4, and moved to North Carolina.

“He had more experience with babies, so he taught me everything,” Ms. Swinton said. “He was an amazing father. He was always my daughter’s favorite.”

Ms. Swinton left the Army in 2023, she said. Her husband’s deployments were hard, she added, and his last was the longest they had been apart since they married. But they kept in contact as best they could.

In February, the war began. And this month, she heard the angst creep into Sergeant Swinton’s voice. “When I did see him on videos, he just looked so tired,” Ms. Swinton said. “And he would tell me he wanted to come home so bad.”

Sergeant Swinton’s remains were returned to the United States on Wednesday. Ms. Swinton went to Dover Air Force Base in Delaware to see the flag-draped caskets of her husband and the three other young Army soldiers. She met President Trump, who she said spoke warmly of her husband’s service.

Ms. Swinton felt both supported and overwhelmed, she said, as she watched her daughter grapple with the meaning of death. “When they were transferring Michael, she said: ‘Is that my Dada in that box?’”

In his remarks, Mr. Trump said that the four soldiers had supported the war. Ms. Swinton said that she would rather talk about her husband than discuss politics.

“Nobody can tell you how a military career will go,” she said. “There’s so much uncertainty, and you have to be strong enough to go along with it and hope that it will turn out OK.”

Sergeant Swinton had hoped that his deployment to Iraq would be his last, Ms. Swinton said, and so had she. “I just wanted to be glued to him,” she said.

“Everything he did — the way he spoke, his voice, everything — I just, I love him,” she said.

Eric Schmitt and Maia Spoto contributed reporting.

item.title: Jackie, Bald Eagle and Webcam Star, Is Recovering After an Attack in California
item.description:
A bald eagle named Jackie, who, with her mate, Shadow, became something of an internet star because of a popular webcam trained on their nest in California, was in critical care this week days after she was attacked by other eagles. The attack helped prompt a rescue that has shed light on unrelated health issues.

The news drew an outpouring of support from people who have gotten to know Jackie since the introduction of a livestream more than a decade ago that captures the nest she shares with Shadow atop a 120-foot-tall Jeffrey pine tree in Big Bear Valley, a lakeside recreation area in Southern California.

The Ojai Raptor Center, the wildlife rehabilitation center in Ojai, Calif., where Jackie was receiving treatment, said in a series of posts on Facebook this week that initial bloodwork showed Jackie was “experiencing severe anemia” and inflammation affecting her kidneys.

In an update on Thursday, the center said her kidney inflammation had improved, but her condition remained critical as a team worked to determine the cause of her anemia.

Jackie also underwent a “successful life-saving transfusion,” the center said, though its post did not specify when. She was described in the post as “eating well, perching, and remains bright and strong.”

The center added that initial testing had ruled out lead toxicosis and the presence of foreign objects such as fishing hooks, lines and weights. She will continue to receive treatment in its urgent care unit, the center said.

“While we are encouraged by the dedication and collaboration surrounding this case, it is still too early to predict the outcome,” the center said on Thursday. “We know many of you are hoping for more answers, and so are we. Wildlife medicine often requires patience, and some answers simply take time.”

The center said it would continue to share information on social media. It did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Thursday.

Nearly a week ago, Jackie was rescued near Dana Point Park on Big Bear Lake.

According to Facebook posts from Friends of Big Bear Valley, the nonprofit organization that operates the camera, an eagle was first spotted on the ground in the area on July 17. The eagle, later identified as Jackie, was then seen engaged in an “altercation” with two sub-adult eagles, the organization said. Cellphone video footage of the altercation showed that Jackie was unable to fly away but fended off her attackers by turning over and using her talons, the group said.

Witnesses stayed in the area to monitor Jackie and called several agencies for help.

Duke Blackwood and his wife, Anne, who have a vacation cabin in the Big Bear area, were sitting by their dock on Friday night when Ms. Blackwood saw something coming out of the water that she initially thought was a dog, only to realize it was an eagle, Mr. Blackwood said.

At first it struck them as unusual, but they could see a small fish in Jackie’s mouth, Mr. Blackwood, 67, said.

Later, they saw Jackie with two other eagles, which they thought were her babies, Mr. Blackwood said. Then, around 9:30 p.m., another couple who had also been watching Jackie knocked on the Blackwoods’ cabin door to alert them that something might be wrong with the eagle.

They all walked down to the docks, where Jackie had hopped onto a nearby catamaran, Mr. Blackwood said. They came within about 15 to 20 feet of Jackie, and she didn’t move. She seemed to be in trouble, he said.

“There was no blood. There were no disheveled feathers. There was no scratch mark, no wing that looked out of place,” he said. “She just was still. And you’d shine the light on her, and she’d give you this look, and it’s like, ‘oh my gosh.’”

Neighbors went to get help at the local San Bernardino County fire station in Fawnskin, and firefighters responded.

“That’s our eagle, we’ve got this,” Ms. Blackwood recalled the fire crew saying when they arrived.

Firefighters stayed with Jackie until 2 a.m., when a rescue team from San Dimas Raptor Rescue, a rehabilitation center within the Los Angeles County Department of Parks and Recreation, arrived, Friends of Big Bear Valley said in a post on Facebook.

Jackie was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center on Saturday afternoon, Friends of Big Bear Valley said.

The group said on Thursday that Jackie, who has been given several medications, was alert and was “still being feisty with the staff” at the center.

“She is still in guarded condition and can turn in a moment,” the group said. “Please keep Jackie and the rest of her family in your thoughts, sending positive energy and prayers.”

Jackie, who hatched in the spring of 2012, has shared a nest with Shadow since he showed up in the summer of 2018 and refused to leave, pushing out her then-partner, named Mr. B. In the wild, bald eagles can live up to 25 years or longer.

Shadow has continued to care for their two eaglets, Sandy and Luna, and protect the nest in Jackie’s absence, the Friends of Big Bear Valley said in a Facebook post.

item.title: ICE Contractor Faces Charges in Shooting Outside Colorado Detention Center
item.description:
A man working for an immigration detention center near Denver was charged with assault on Wednesday after shooting at protesters outside the facility last week, hitting a college student in the foot, according to the authorities and the student. He was subsequently fired from his job there.

Brandon Booth, 42, is accused of firing a single shot from his personal pistol on July 16 before driving off from the Immigration Customs and Enforcement processing center in Aurora, Colo., operated by his now-former employer, the GEO Group, according to the city police.

Mr. Booth was arrested nearby shortly afterward. He was charged on Wednesday with first-degree assault and attempted assault, according to county prosecutors. A spokesman for the GEO Group, one of the largest private prison operators in the country, said in a statement on Thursday that Mr. Booth had been “terminated” from his job at the facility.

The shooting happened after two women had “initiated a verbal confrontation” with Mr. Booth and other GEO employees who were in a car waiting out a protest that was “impeding” their way into work, according to the police.

Emma Landis, 21, a college student who has regularly protested outside the facility, said in an interview on Thursday evening that one of the employees had appeared particularly bothered and started yelling back in her direction. As Ms. Landis and a friend walked away, the employee fired a shot, hitting her in the foot, she said.

“My leg went really numb and started burning,” Ms. Landis said. “I laid down and there was blood dripping from my foot, and I called 911.”

Mr. Booth appeared in court on Wednesday and as of late Thursday was being held in the Adams County Jail on $100,000 bond, according to a jail employee. It was not immediately clear on Thursday night whether he had a lawyer.

Among the ICE processing centers operated by the GEO Group is Delaney Hall in New Jersey, where federal agents have clashed with people protesting President Trump’s immigration crackdown. Detainees at the center, in Newark, have complained for months about dirty, unhealthy living conditions. Members of Congress have stepped up their criticism of the facility.

Ms. Landis said the demonstrations at Delaney Hall had driven her to join those outside the GEO-operated Aurora facility, which have often brought out much smaller crowds of protesters. She described the shooting as “coming out of nowhere.”

And she planned to return to protests on Thursday on crutches.
